govdocs-archive_org-jors195320fppng_v03_:
Vannevar Bush ran American science during the Second World War, heading the office that put radar, the proximity fuze, and the atomic bomb program into motion. Research and the War Effort, his piece in the Operational Research Society's journal, looks back at that mobilization.

Bush describes how thousands of scientists were drawn into war work and what their research changed on the battlefield and at sea. He writes as the administrator who built the system, plain about both its triumphs and its friction with the military. The piece is a primary source on wartime science policy by the man who directed it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HochPaulHSCANot:
Paul L. Hoch drafted a commentary on the House Select Committee on Assassinations hearings in October and November 1978. The piece was a first draft prepared for Inquiry magazine. Hoch followed the hearings as a researcher who knew the files, grading the committee's work as it unfolded in public.

A first draft is a mind not yet polished for print. Hoch's comments show what an informed skeptic made of the testimony day by day. Prepared for a magazine of inquiry, the draft preserves the research community's running verdict on the second great assassination investigation.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
Vladimir Putin first won election as president of Russia in March 2000, after Boris Yeltsin handed him power at the end of 1999. Twenty-four years later, in March 2024, the National Security Archive published declassified American records looking back at that vote and at how United States officials judged it at the time.

One declassified record quoted in the posting calls the 2000 election reasonably free and fair. That judgment sits at the heart of the release, since Putin's later elections drew far harsher charges from Western governments. Readers get the early American view in the officials' own words, from a moment when ties between Washington and Moscow were warmer and the new Russian leader was still an open question.
grand-grimoire-french:
Le Grand Grimoire, the Grand Grimoire, is the most famous black book of the French tradition. This French text belongs to the nineteenth century, when printed copies spread widely. Its other name, the Red Dragon, comes from the title under which many copies traveled through France.

At its center stands a pact with Lucifuge Rofocale, a chief spirit of hell. The magician signs away his soul and names his price, in the book's own chilling bargain. That scene defined the grimoire tradition for popular imagination. Treasure hunting, spirit service, and dire warnings fill the pages. No French grimoire has cast a longer shadow, for better or worse.
grimorium-verum-french:
The Grimorium Verum, the True Grimoire, survives here in its classic French text of about 1817. It claims descent from Solomon, like most books of its kind. The French version became the standard one, a concise manual of spirits, seals, and pacts that working magicians actually used.

Its pages teach the conjurer how to prepare, which spirits to call, and what seals to draw. The tone is practical, brief, and dark. The book anchored the eighteenth-century French grimoire trade that peddlers carried across Europe. Unlike the vast learned tomes, the Grimorium Verum fits a pocket and a purpose. Generations of magicians passed it from hand to hand.
hilgers-die-bucherverbote-in-papstbriefe: Die Bücherverbote in Papstbriefen, kanonistisch-bibliographische Studie, by Hilgers. The papal book bans. This book preserves that study. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
indian-frontier-policy-an-historical-ske:
General Sir John Adye's Indian Frontier Policy is a historical sketch of Britain's policy on India's north-west frontier. Adye writes while military operations on a considerable scale are under way against a combination of independent tribes along the frontier.

He insists that the troubles are no sudden outbreak, but the consequence of events in bygone years, and he offers a short summary of their varying phases. Contents begin with events before and including the first Afghan war of 1839 to 1841, and the proposed invasion of India by Napoleon. Adye hopes his summary will help the public understand the bearings of policy and judge what should be pursued. Readers of imperial history will find it concise and soldierly.
indian-games-an-historical-research:
Andrew McFarland Davis's Indian Games is a historical research into the games of North America's native peoples. Davis begins with Father Brebeuf's 1636 account of the Hurons, who prized three games above others: cross, platter and straw.

Brebeuf marvelled that a sick man, hot with fever, might be ordered a game of cross as his only cooling remedy. Villages would array themselves against each other in a beautiful field, wagering beaver skins to raise the excitement. Davis traces these games and their meanings through the early accounts, treating play as medicine, ritual and social contest at once. Students of native history and of the history of sport will find it a careful, source-based study.
jack-ranger-s-western-trip-or-from-board:
Clarence Young's Jack Ranger's Western Trip takes its hero from boarding school to ranch and range. The story opens at Washington Hall, where Jack falls into trouble, faces a threatening letter, and turns tables on a plot with a chemistry lesson.

A burglar scare, Nat's invitation, and a grand wind-up send Jack west, where an old acquaintance, Professor Punjab's trick, and shooting an oil well await. The wild steer, the old stockman, a thief in the night, a cattle stampede, and hunting mountain lions follow. Young readers who enjoy school stories that become western adventures will find Jack Ranger brisk and cheerful.
judith-of-blue-lake-ranch:
Judith of Blue Lake Ranch is a Western novel by Jackson Gregory, published in March 1919 by Charles Scribner's Sons. W. Herbert Dunton drew the pictures. The frontispiece shows Judith's spurs turning a bucking, devil-hearted horse. Twenty chapters are listed, opening with Bud Lee Wants to Know.

Judith takes a hand, rides an outlaw, and puts matters straight in the early chapters. Later titles promise rifle shots from cliffs, a happening in Squaw Creek Cañon, and time under fire in an old cabin. Young Hampton registers a protest, and a partners theme closes the list shown. Gregory writes ranch adventure with a heroine who rides and decides for herself.
laennec-auscultation-mediate-vol1-1819-f:
French readers met Laennec's invention in its first form in De l'auscultation mediate, printed in 1819. Tome one opens the treatise on diagnosing diseases of the lungs and heart. Laennec describes the stethoscope, a simple wooden tube of his own devising. He then sets out the sounds it reveals and what each one means.

Healthy and sick chests are compared sound by sound. Laennec writes from hospital wards, testing each sign against what autopsies later showed. That link between sound and lesion made his method scientific. The French first edition is the founding text of chest examination. A separate English translation by Forbes is also held.
laennec-auscultation-mediate-vol2-1819-f:
Tome two of Laennec's De l'auscultation mediate, also from 1819, completes the original French treatise. The first tome set out the stethoscope and its basic signs. The second carries the method through the diseases of the lungs and heart in full. Case evidence and lesion records fill its pages.

Laennec matches what the ear hears to what the opened body shows. That discipline turned listening into diagnosis. French medicine gained a tool that spread across the world within years. The two tomes together form one work and should be read as such. This second half holds much of the clinical detail. It rewards doctors and historians alike.
language-an-introduction-to-the-study-of:
Edward Sapir published Language in 1921, as an introduction to the study of speech. Nine chapters move from a definition of language to its history. Sapir calls language a cultural act, not an inborn one.

He rejects simple theories that speech began with cries or sound copying. Chapters treat sounds, words, grammar, and how languages change. He also asks whether thought is possible without language. Sapir writes for general readers, not only scholars. His book remains a classic doorway into linguistics, the science of language. Sapir's examples come from many tongues, including Native American languages. They show how widely human speech patterns can differ.
lois-the-witch:
Elizabeth Gaskell's story of Lois appears in this 1861 work. A modern Penguin introduction traces Gaskell's life first. She was born in London in 1810, it explains. Cheshire, Stratford, and the north formed her early years.

In 1832 she married the Reverend William Gaskell of Manchester. Household, parish work, and motherhood filled sixteen busy years. Mary Barton, her first full fiction, succeeded instantly in 1848. Charlotte Brontë became her close friend from 1850 onward. Dickens's Household Words carried her fiction for thirteen years. North and South, another Manchester novel, appeared in 1855. She also wrote for Dickens's magazine Household Words over thirteen years.
madam-how-and-lady-why-or-first-lessons-:
Madam How and Lady Why gives first lessons in earth lore for children. Charles Kingsley wrote it, and this text follows the 1889 Macmillan edition. He dedicated it to his son Grenville Arthur and his schoolfellows. His preface scolds the dull, ugly children's books of his own boyhood.

Kingsley urges boys to use their eyes, ears, and common sense. Madam How and Lady Why are his two guiding figures. One shows how things happen; the other asks why they happen. Volcanoes, tides, fossils, and cliffs become stories under their lead. Kingsley was a clergyman who loved natural science deeply. His book taught wonder first and facts close behind.
mrs-piper-the-society-for-psychical-rese:
Michael Sage wrote this study of Mrs. Piper, a famed trance medium. Noralie Robertson translated it from French, slightly cut. Sir Oliver Lodge wrote the preface for the 1904 New York edition. The book asks if mediumship is a sickness of the nerves.

Chapters weigh fraud, muscle reading, and thought transfer as rival claims. Professor William James of Harvard watched her early trances with care. Dr. Richard Hodgson led much of the research. A full sitting with Mrs. Piper is set out for readers. The book is a calm, close look at the science of ghosts in its early days.
mrs-wiggs-of-the-cabbage-patch:
Alice Caldwell Hegan Rice wrote this tale of a poor city district, copyrighted in 1901. She dedicated it to her mother, angel of the Cabbage Patch. The contents open with Mrs. Wiggs's philosophy. Ways and means, a Christmas lady, and a benefit dance follow.

Mrs. Wiggs keeps cheer in a hard place and helps her neighbors. A theater party and Mr. Bob bring town folk into the Patch. One chapter tells how spring came to the district. Rice writes poverty with humor and respect, not pity. The small book won wide love for its claim that joy can live on very little.
nasa-tm-19650019857-highlights-of-recent:
Robert Jastrow is named in the surviving pages of this survey of recent space research. Space science, he writes, is not one field by itself. It draws on Earth sciences, physics, and astronomy, where spacecraft can do what ground experiments cannot. In later years, he adds, the life sciences would join that group in a major role.

Jastrow links that growth to exploration of the Moon and planets. The survey reviews work in the physical sciences and discusses it for a broad reader. As a snapshot, it shows how a leading space scientist framed the field while the first wave of spacecraft results was still fresh.
nasa-tm-19660020064-advances-in-particle:
W Hess, G Mead, and M P Nakada of Goddard's Theoretical Division reviewed gains in particles and fields research in January 1965. Their era is the satellite age, counted from 1958. Subjects include the solar wind's effect on Earth and the radiation belts. Earth's magnetic field, solar energetic particles, and cosmic rays all receive treatment, along with neutrons and ground effects.

Before satellites, most of these topics rested on hints from the ground. Seven years of flight data had remade the field. A review by three of its workers marks the change in one place. It also tells later readers exactly what was known, and what was still guesswork, at that early date.
nasa-tm-19670012812-radiometry-research:
The Radiometry Section at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland issued this summary in February 1967. Radiometry is the science of measuring radiation, and the section supported spacecraft work. The report sums up the section's activities for the latter part of 1966.

It is divided into three parts. One covers work by the section's own staff, and the others cover on-site and off-site contractor work. The catalog record lists work on spacecraft coatings and solar simulators. It also names vortex arc studies, measurements of solar flux and spectra, and tests of radiation effects on solar cells.
nasa-tm-19690028207-cloud-statistics-in-:
Vincent V. Salomonson wrote this Goddard preprint, numbered X-622-69-386, on cloud statistics for Earth Resources Technology Satellite mission planning. ERTS craft, due in the early nineteen seventies, would map mineral, ocean, water, and farm resources from orbit. Their sensors need clear skies, so planners need to know how often any given place is actually cloud free.

Few studies give cloud cover as a frequency distribution over place and time, Salomonson finds. Those few show only small portions of Earth clear often enough for good odds on repeated passes. Over the United States, fall viewing is best and spring viewing worst. He also warns that satellite sensors misjudge broken cumulus and thin cirrus in opposite directions.
nasa-tm-19700015897-magnetometers-for-sp:
Norman F. Ness wrote this review in March 1970, while on leave from the Goddard Space Flight Center. He was based at a plasma laboratory in Rome, Italy. His subject is magnetometers, the tools spacecraft carry to measure magnetic fields in space.

Ness opens with a short summary of major results gained with these tools. He then explains how each main type works. The types covered are search coil, fluxgate, proton, alkali vapor, and helium vapor instruments. He closes with how the tools are tested and calibrated. The review served builders and users of field-measuring gear on space missions.
nasa-tm-19700025444-a-simulated-study-of:
Ronald W. Simpson wrote this Apollo study of manual control techniques for lunar orbit rendezvous. It is a simulation study, run with the concentrated flight plan for that rendezvous. Crews would need such hand-flying skills if automatic systems fell short near the Moon, far from any quick help.

The study grows out of earlier work on backup monitoring and control for rendezvous flights. Those efforts asked how a crew could watch the primary guidance system and step in after a partial or complete failure. A recent guidance division simulation had tested control modes that might back up the primary system. Simpson's runs apply that thinking to the tighter, concentrated plan for meeting in lunar orbit.
nasa-tm-19710006420-summer-institute-for:
The Goddard Space Flight Center issued this final report in January 1971. It closes out the Summer Institute for Biomedical Research in Technology Utilization. The institute ran from June 22 to August 28, 1970.

The program brought space technology into medical work. NASA instruments built to watch astronauts could also watch patients. The report covers both the running of the institute and its technical side. It is classed as an administrative and technical report, the closing record of the session. Programs of this kind were NASA's way of paying back its research cost in daily life.
orchesography-or-the-art-of-dancing-the-: Orchesography is John Weaver's 1706 English translation of Raoul-Auger Feuillet's French manual of baroque dance notation. It was printed in London. Its title promises the whole art explained through characters and demonstrative figures. Tables of steps and rules for the arms are also promised. The hosted sample contains only the title page. A transcriber's note warns that the work leans so heavily on diagrams that no plain text version exists. The steps themselves cannot be read here.
poor-miss-finch:
Wilkie Collins dedicated Poor Miss Finch to Mrs. Elliot of the Deanery, Bristol, in memory of an uninterrupted friendship, and used his preface to state a daring aim. Fiction had shown charming blind girls before, he writes, but always from the ideal and sentimental side; his Lucilla would exhibit blindness as it really is. Collins gathered his facts from competent authorities, and everything Lucilla does or says about her condition rests on what blind people had actually done and said.

Around Lucilla he built an intricate plot of love, identity, and deception, with the twin Nugent Dubourg and the narrator Madame Pratolungo as studies in human inconsistency. Collins argues in the preface that readers wrongly demand logical consistency from fictional motives. The novel, part sensation story and part serious experiment, asks sympathy for its heroine without a drop of the usual syrup.
racine-mithridate-french:
Racine's Mithridate, a tragedy of 1673 in French, stages the last days of a famed king. The cast lists Mithridate, king of Pontus, with Monime, promised to him and named queen. His sons Pharnace and Xiphares, born of different mothers, stand beside them.

The scene is Nymphee, a seaport on the Cimmerian Bosphorus. In his preface Racine notes that Sulla, Lucullus, and Pompey won glory against this foe. Old and beaten, the king still schemes, famed for guarding himself against poison. A love triangle in his shadow sharpens this most political of Racine's plays, a study of pride facing ruin.
racketty-packetty-house-as-told-by-queen:
Racketty-Packetty House, as told by Queen Crosspatch, is a children's story by Frances Hodgson Burnett, with illustrations by Harrison Cady. Queen Crosspatch begins with a rule: dolls do anything they choose when people are not looking, dancing, singing, and playing the piano, but they stop the moment anyone turns to watch.

The house of the title stands in a corner of Cynthia's nursery, behind the door, the worst spot in the room. It was pushed there when Tidy Castle arrived for Cynthia's birthday. Tidy Castle is a grand new dolls' house. It has elegant furniture and a knocker on the door. Cynthia is ashamed of the shabby old house beside it.
samuel-butler-a-sketch:
Henry Festing Jones wrote Samuel Butler: A Sketch to introduce the life of the writer Samuel Butler. The piece first appeared in 1913 inside a Butler essay volume and came out again from Jonathan Cape in London in 1921. Jones had already written a full memoir of Butler, and the sketch gives the family background in short form.

Butler was born on December 4, 1835, at Langar Rectory in Nottinghamshire, where his father Thomas then served as rector. His mother, Fanny Worsley, came from a Bristol sugar family, and his grandfather had led Shrewsbury School before becoming Bishop of Lichfield. Jones stresses that these Butlers were kin to neither the Hudibras poet nor the Analogy writer. Butler's schooldays began at home, and a family trip to Italy in 1843 gave the boy, at eight, his first great event.
slips-of-speech:
John H. Bechtel wrote Slips of Speech to help readers fix the day-to-day faults of speech and writing. Bechtel, also the author of Practical Synonyms and a work on how words are said, saw the book printed at Philadelphia by the Penn Publishing Company in 1901, under an 1895 copyright. Chapters treat taste, choice of words, short forms, the possessive case, pronouns, and number.

Later chapters cover adverbs, word links, the infinitive, participles, and small words of place and time. Redundancy, two negatives, and the match of verb with subject close the list, with an index at the end. Bechtel opens by noting that Homer knew no rules yet wrote verse that lasts. Most men, he argues, are no Homer, and so they need rules to guide them.
stories-about-animals-with-pictures-to-m:
Francis C. Woodworth, editor of The Youth's Cabinet and author of Stories About Birds, published Stories About Animals, With Pictures to Match at Boston in 1851; the work was entered for copyright in 1849. His preface says the pages group together short accounts chosen to show animal character.

Woodworth wrote for young readers, pairing each story with a picture so the lesson lands twice. The tales draw out traits like faithfulness, cleverness, and kindness in common and wild creatures. Books of this kind taught children natural history through story rather than dry lists, and Woodworth's plain, warm style made him a steady name in American homes.
the-arctic-prairies-a-canoe-journey-of-2:
Ernest Thompson Seton, billed as author of Wild Animals I Have Known, recounts a canoe journey of two thousand miles in search of the caribou. The book is dedicated to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, premier of Canada. Its subtitle calls it an account of a voyage to the region north of Aylmer Lake.

Seton's preface asks what young man would not give a year of his life to roll back time five decades. He dreams of the old Missouri with buffalo on its banks, big game in sight, and red men roaming free of fences. Trading posts stood hundreds of miles apart then, he notes, and news moved by horse or canoe. His own northern trip, he hints, bought a share of that lost world at far less cost.
the-boy-life-of-napoleon-afterwards-empe:
Boy Life of Napoleon, Afterwards Emperor of the French, came out in 1895 with art by Vesper L. George. It was adapted and made larger for American boys and girls from the French work of Madame Eugénie Foa. Foa had written Little Princes and Princesses and Little Robinson. A preface tells how her name had been known in French homes for more than a generation.

The preface praises Foa as the most loved French writer of tales from past times for the young, some forty years back. Her tone is pure, her morals high, and her teaching direct, it says. It also credits her with true facts and strong action. For this form, new study was drawn on to round out her sketch of Napoleon's boyhood. The hope is that young readers will go on to his later life with minds free of party bias, hate, and hero worship.
the-delights-of-wisdom-pertaining-to-con:
Emanuel Swedenborg, named on the title page as a Swede, wrote The Delights of Wisdom Pertaining to Conjugial Love, with The Pleasures of Insanity Pertaining to Scortatory Love added. The English text translates his Latin work printed at Amsterdam in 1768. The opening relations concern the joys of heaven and weddings there.

Swedenborg solemnly declares that what follows is no fiction of the imagination. He says the scenes were truly done and seen, not in sleep but in full wakefulness. The Lord opened the inner parts of his mind and spirit. He was granted to be in the spiritual world with angels and in the natural world with men at once, for twenty-five years as of 1768. An angel then appears beneath the eastern heaven, sounding a trumpet toward the north, the west, and the south.
the-flying-u-ranch:
B. M. Bower wrote Flying U Ranch as a western tale of the Happy Family, a crew of cowhands on a Montana ranch. Sheep trouble stands near the heart of the contents.

The tale opens as the crew waits for Sunday supper at the bunkhouse door. The Old Man comes back from Helena with a stranger, Miguel Rapponi, a flashy dresser straight from San Francisco. The boys eye his silk scarf, stamped cuffs, and high boot heels with one mind of doubt. Sheep camps, false friends, and range pride test the crew's trust in the books that follow.
the-fourth-watch: H. A. Cody wrote The Fourth Watch as a novel of a clergyman's life, and only the front matter and contents are present here. Cody gives the book to the watchmen and stewards of the Lord who toil through life's long night. The chapter heads name Glendow Rectory, the breath of slander, an auction, a golden key, camp scenes, a long night, and light at eventide. Cody's past books named here include The Frontiersman and The Long Patrol. No chapter text appears in these opening pages.
the-golden-calf-which-the-world-adores-a: John Frederick Helvetius wrote The Golden Calf, Which the World Adores and Desires. Helvetius was a doctor at the Hague. The tract was first set down in Latin. It is here faithfully Englished. John Starkey printed it in London in 1670. Only front matter is present here: the long title page and dedications. The title page states the claim of the tract. At the Hague in 1666, the whole substance of lead was changed in one moment. It became gold-obrizon. A tiny grain of the true philosophick stone did the work.
the-house-of-heine-brothers-in-munich:
A small Munich banking firm sits at the center of this story. The text comes from the 1864 Chapman and Hall edition of Tales of All Countries. The Heine brothers keep a modest office in the old market-place. Only three clerks work there. One old man never deals with the public. A young Englishman assists him. A boy runs messages and tends the stoves. Nobody doubts the brothers' word or their solvency. Their business is tiny beside the great London banks.

London houses employ legions of clerks. Their partners stay hidden from customers. The Heines instead sit visibly in two dingy rooms. A broad staircase leads up to them. The elder brother is a bachelor in the suburbs. The younger, Ernest Heine, has a wife much younger than himself. They have two daughters and a son. Firm and family stand side by side. The story is ready to entangle them.
the-immortals-masterpieces-of-fiction-cr: Project Gutenberg's 1905 edition of the French Immortals gathers nineteen novels crowned by the French Academy, each also issued separately. the-lighted-match: Charles Neville Buck published his novel with W. J. Watt in New York in 1911, illustrated by R. F. Schabelitz. The first chapter listed is called An Omen Is Construed. The novel itself, a Kentucky mountain romance by the author of The Key to Yesterday, does not appear here.
the-man-who-knew-too-much:
Gilbert K. Chesterton's The Man Who Knew Too Much gathers eight detective tales. They include The Face in the Target, The Vanishing Prince, The Soul of the Schoolboy, and The Bottomless Well. The Fad of the Fisherman, The Hole in the Wall, The Temple of Silence, and The Vengeance of the Statue follow. The first story sends Harold March, a rising reviewer and social critic, walking briskly across a great tableland of moors toward Torwood Park. March is on a political errand: the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Sir Howard Horne, will expound his so-called Socialist budget to him in an interview.

March knows all about politics and nothing about politicians, Chesterton says, and much about art and philosophy, but little about the world he lives in. Midway across the sunny flats he finds a narrow cleft carrying a small stream, and curiosity pulls him down into it.
the-master-detective-being-some-further-:
Percy James Brebner published The Master Detective in 1916, a set of further investigations by his sleuth Christopher Quarles. Fifteen cases fill the contents, from a kidnapping and a stolen aeroplane model to a contessa's pearls and a crime in a yellow taxi. Other cases involve a jeweled chalice, a forty-ton yawl, and the Grange Park mystery. The first case opens with the death of Sir Grenville Rusholm, baronet.

Obituary notices fill the papers, wreaths crowd the Lodge in Queen's Square, and Lady Rusholm receives floods of sympathy. Brebner notes that the dead man counted for little in politics, having refused to stand for Parliament. His social success owed much, perhaps, to his wife's charm. Yet a man so prominent leaves questions behind him when he dies. Quarles steps into a world of wealth, reputation, and hidden difficulty.
the-miller-of-old-church: Ellen Glasgow's novel The Miller of Old Church shows only its dedication and contents here, so the story itself does not appear. Glasgow dedicated the book to her sister Cary Glasgow McCormack, in loving acknowledgment of help and sympathy through the years. The contents divide the novel into Jordan's Journey and The Cross-Roads. Chapter titles promise a mill, a flirtatious Molly, a sermon by the Reverend Orlando Mullen, and chapters treating the ladies' sphere, contradictions, and life's ironies.
the-moon-out-of-reach:
Margaret Pedler's novel The Moon Out of Reach holds a 1921 copyright. Grosset and Dunlap published it in New York. Only title page and contents are present here, so the story does not appear. Pedler is billed as author of The House of Dreams-Come-True, The Splendid Folly, and The Lamp of Fate.

Eighteen chapters are listed. The Shining Ship and The Good Samaritan open the book, followed by A Question of Externals and The Skeleton in the Cupboard. Preux Chevalier, A Forgotten Fan, and The Other Side of the Door lead toward A Skirmish with Death. By the Lovers' Bridge, Relations-in-Law, King Arthur's Castle, and Till Death Us Do Part close the list on a romantic note.
the-old-peabody-pew-a-christmas-romance-: A Christmas romance of a country church, The Old Peabody Pew appeared in a 1907 edition. No author is named in the pages present here, which hold the dedication only, so the story itself does not appear. The dedication speaks to New England women of a quiet village who worked with the writer in a Dorcas Society, and recalls their white-spired meeting house. The writer admits there never was a Peabody Pew, and offers the imagined tale back with rosemary, for remembrance.
the-personal-touch: J. Wilbur Chapman, D.D., wrote The Personal Touch, a book on personal evangelism. The pages present hold the contents and the opening of a foreword headed simply "If," so the chapters themselves do not appear. The contents list A Testimony, A General Principle, No Man Cared for My Soul, Winning the Young, and Conversion Is a Miracle. The foreword argues that if being a Christian is worthwhile, ordinary concern should prompt us to speak of Christ to those we meet.
the-slowcoach:
E. V. Lucas's The Slowcoach runs to twenty-four chapters, its contents say. The Avories open the book. Mysterious wheels, a thorough examination, and the plans follow. The first day and first night of travel come at chapters eight and nine. Adventures punctuate the list: a second caravan, a young policeman, runaway ponies, and a lost baby. Stratford-on-Avon appears at chapter twelve. The most surprising adventure of all precedes the end.

Chapter one introduces the Avory family in an old house at Chiswick. Once upon a time there was a nice family, Lucas begins. Captain Avory was dead, wounded at Spion Kop, the narrator explains. Mrs. Avory was thirty-five, with four children. Janet, aged fourteen, was the eldest, and Gregory Bruce, aged seven, the youngest. They were all very fond of each other, Lucas adds.
the-true-story-of-my-life-a-sketch: Hans Christian Andersen's True Story of My Life, a sketch translated by Mary Howitt, is introduced in this record by Howitt's own letter to her Boston publishers, dated London, 29 June 1847. She forwards the proof sheets of Andersen's unpublished life, translated from a copy the author sent her, and notes that this is the author's edition, in whose proceeds he shares. The translation is inscribed to Jenny Lind, in admiration of her talents and her beautiful life. Andersen's autobiography itself begins after these formal leaves.
the-vagabond-and-other-poems-from-punch: R. C. Lehmann collected The Vagabond and Other Poems from Punch in a volume published by John Lane in 1918. The poems themselves are not present in this record; the note and contents list are what appear. Titles include The Vagabond, Singing Water, Cragwell End, The Bird in the Room, and Killed in Action. Later entries name a poem to Flight-Lieutenant Robinson, V. C.
the-way-of-salvation-in-the-lutheran-chu: G. H. Gerberding wrote The Way of Salvation in the Lutheran Church for a Lutheran Publication Society edition in Philadelphia. the-yoke-a-romance-of-the-days-when-the-: Elizabeth Miller's The Yoke, copyrighted in 1904, is presented here by its title pages and contents. thomas-henry-huxley-a-character-sketch: Leonard Huxley wrote a character sketch of his father, Thomas Henry Huxley, issued for the Rationalist Press Association and published by Watts in London in 1920. thomas-jefferson-a-character-sketch:
Edward S. Ellis wrote a character sketch of Thomas Jefferson for the Great Americans of History series, with a supplementary essay by G. Mercer Adam. The volume also promises an account of the Louisiana Purchase, anecdotes, characteristics, and a chronology. Ellis compares Jefferson's mark on early government to a mint stamp.

He calls Jefferson an aristocrat by birth and a democrat by nature, learned yet fond of a farmer's simple tastes. Jefferson refused birthday celebrations and disliked titles and ceremony. Readers get an admiring popular biography built from traits, stories, and praise for his foresight about the young nation.
three-frenchmen-in-bengal-the-commercial: S. C. Hill, officer in charge of the records of the Government of India, published Three Frenchmen in Bengal in 1903. His subtitle names the commercial ruin of the French settlements in 1757. Maps and plans accompany the book, including the Ganges valley after Rennell. Four chapters treat the quarrel with the English, then Renault at Chandernagore, Law at Cossimbazar, and Courtin at Dacca. Hill dedicated the work to his wife. The front pages and contents are what is held in this record, so Hill's history itself is not shown.
tillie-a-mennonite-maid-a-story-of-the-p: Helen Reimensnyder Martin wrote a story of the Pennsylvania Dutch, and its contents list twenty-six chapters in the characters' own dialect. Later headings promise Tillie's revolt, her last fight, and Getz learning Tillie. Chapter one is announced with the cry Oh, I love her, but no text follows. The contents pages are what is given in this record, so Martin's novel itself is not shown.
un-doc-yasser-arafat-s-1974-un-general-a:
Yasser Arafat, leader of the Palestine Liberation Organization, addressed the United Nations General Assembly in November 1974. No Palestinian leader had spoken to the Assembly before. The hall heard him say he had come bearing an olive branch and a freedom fighter's gun, and he begged the world not to let the branch fall.

The speech argues that Palestinians are a people with a right to their own state. It rejects the label of terrorist and blames the conflict on dispossession. The address won the PLO observer status at the UN and stands as a landmark of Palestinian diplomacy.
what-the-schools-teach-and-might-teach: The opening shown here is made up of the title page and lists of tables, so Franklin Bobbitt's findings do not appear.
